quote: 14.1 Assignment. Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent, except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.
rationale: Section 14.1 is the only assignment provision, and no clause anywhere gives Commerce One a termination or re-pricing right on Corio's change of control (§ 11 termination triggers are breach and insolvency only), so we are outside walk-away territory. The clause already delivers two fallback elements mutually: successor assignment in a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all related assets without consent, and a consent requirement for all other assignments. It fails the fallback on two material terms: the consent requirement carries no reasonableness standard (so Commerce One could refuse an affiliate or other assignment arbitrarily), and the successor carve-out has no written-notice mechanic. We therefore propose the two shortest conforming edits to bring § 14.1 to the fallback level, leaving the mutual direct-competitor consent proviso and the null-and-void sentence untouched. We have not sought the preferred affiliate carve-out, since a no-consent affiliate exception is inconsistent with the fallback requirement that all non-successor assignments need consent.

Note two retained narrowings: the asset test is limited to assets "related to this Agreement", and consent is still required where the transaction involves a direct competitor of Vendor; the added "upon prior written notice" is a notice, not a consent, condition.

verification.notes: Fallback level is complete: mutual successor right (retained), prior written notice (added), consent for all other assignments (retained), and a reasonableness standard on that consent (added). Preferred level is not reached: no affiliate no-consent carve-out for Customer, Vendor retains a no-consent successor assignment right, and the competitor restriction is consent-based rather than an absolute bar on assignment to a Customer competitor. Correctly not pursued, since a Customer affiliate exception would collide with the fallback element requiring consent for all non-successor assignments. Deviation status is right: before the edit the clause failed the fallback on two material terms (no reasonableness standard on consent, no notice mechanic for the successor carve-out); it is not walk-away because there is a mutual M&A carve-out and no Vendor termination or re-pricing right on Customer's change of control. Minimal: two short in-line insertions, no deletions, no survival tails, expense language, or procedures; the favourable retained language (mutual competitor-consent proviso, null-and-void sentence, successors-and-assigns sentence) is untouched. Preserves intent: mutuality, the competitor proviso, and the invalidity remedy all survive without contradiction; no undefined terms or dangling cross-references are created. Minor residual worth noting in the rationale only (not a deviation): the added reasonableness standard sits in the first sentence and arguably does not reach the separate competitor-consent proviso, and the asset test remains "assets related to this Agreement" rather than all assets.

verification.notes: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative rendered text: 90-day Software-to-Documentation warranty, the same 90-day period for the MarketSite.net Service (above the 30-day floor), correction/free replacement, and a refund of all prepaid fees. Preferred level is not reached: no professional-and-workmanlike services standard, no compliance-with-laws warranty, and the software period is 90 days rather than 12 months. These are noted, not required, because the fallback is complete. Minimality holds. Only two edits were made inside the target element: sixty (60) → ninety (90), and deletion of "but in no event not later than December 31, 1999". The outside date deletion is necessary rather than cosmetic — with an Effective Date of 29 October 1999, a 31 December 1999 cap would have cut the period to roughly 63 days and contradicted the extension. No survival tail, expense language, extra remedies or boilerplate were added. Intent is preserved. The defined term "Warranty Period" is retained and still anchors the malicious-code warranty, the media-replacement sentence, the correction/refund cascade, the sole-and-exclusive-remedies sentence and the exclusions list; no cross-reference is left dangling and no retained sentence now contradicts the 90-day period. The underlying finding of deviation is correct: at 60 days (further truncated by the 31 December 1999 cap) the original Software conformance warranty fell below the 90-day fallback floor, which is a material term rather than a minor sub-element.

quote: Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year, at reasonable times and upon reasonable notice. Commerce One shall bear all costs and expenses of such inspection.
rationale: Section 4.4 is the only audit right binding Corio (no audit/inspection language appears in Exhibit B pricing, revenue-share or payment terms). It already sits at or above the fallback on most terms: inspections are limited to once each calendar year, are performed by an independent certified public accountant reasonably acceptable to Corio, are confined to books and records verifying amounts payable (no access to Corio systems), and Commerce One bears all costs unless an underpayment of more than 5% is found — the same cost threshold the playbook accepts at the preferred level. The single fallback element it fails is the notice quantum: "reasonable notice" sets no minimum and leaves timing at Commerce One's discretion, so we have fixed it at 15 days with a one-phrase edit. Remaining preferred-only refinements (30 days' notice, express business-hours and off-site wording, auditor confidentiality undertaking) are noted but not pressed.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: Retained: "Such inspections may be made no more than once each calendar year" — an express annual frequency cap satisfying the fallback (which does not require a rolling 12-month measure).

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Operation 1 replaces open-ended "reasonable notice" with "upon at least 15 days' notice", fixing a hard minimum notice period exactly at the fallback quantum.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: "Commerce One shall bear all costs and expenses of such inspection", with cost-shifting only on an underpayment "of more than five percent (5%)". Vendor-borne cost is expressly allocated and the shifting trigger is the 5% figure the playbook itself specifies at the preferred level, so the cost-allocation element is satisfied; note the retained 5% (rather than 10%) trigger shifts cost to Customer somewhat sooner than the fallback figure if the team wants to press it.

verification.notes: Position-complete at the fallback: frequency (once each calendar year) and Vendor-borne cost with a 5% underpayment trigger were already in Section 4.4, and the single gap — an indeterminate "reasonable notice" with no floor — is closed by the inserted "at least 15 days' notice". Preferred level is not reached: notice is 15 rather than 30 days and not stated to be written; there is no business-hours limitation (only "at reasonable times"), no off-site preference, no auditor confidentiality undertaking, and the frequency cap is calendar-year rather than any rolling 12-month period. These are correctly noted rather than pressed, but the level must not be marked complete. Minimal: exactly one phrase is changed within the notice element ("upon reasonable notice" -> "upon at least 15 days' notice"). Favourable retained language — annual cap, independent CPA reasonably acceptable to Customer, Vendor cost-bearing, books-and-records-only scope, the reciprocal shortfall/overpayment true-up and the 3-year retention period — is untouched, and no survival tail, procedure or extra requirement outside the checklist is added. Preserves intent: the audit's purpose (verifying amounts payable), the reciprocal payment/refund mechanic and the 5% reimbursement trigger all survive without contradiction; no undefined term or dangling cross-reference is created, and "at reasonable times" still coexists coherently with the new fixed notice period. Optional hardening if the counterparty engages: add "written" before notice and, if the team wants literal fallback parity on cost, raise the reimbursement trigger from 5% to 10%; neither is required for fallback completeness as scored here. Severity is reduced to low: the clause sat at or above the fallback on every material term except the notice floor, and the walk-away triggers (unlimited/unannounced audits, system access) were never present.
